title: Adrenal Disorders: Insufficiency, Adrenal Crisis & Cushing Syndrome
html:
Cortisol helps maintain vascular response to stress, glucose availability, and normal metabolism. Aldosterone helps retain sodium and water while excreting potassium. Too little effective cortisol can become a rapidly fatal adrenal crisis; prolonged cortisol excess causes multisystem harm. The RN's work is to recognize patterns, protect circulation, verify steroid therapy, identify triggers, and help clients follow a workable emergency plan.

Learning goals

  • Distinguish primary from central or glucocorticoid-induced adrenal insufficiency.
  • Recognize adrenal crisis and prioritize emergency stabilization.
  • Explain daily hormone replacement, illness-related dose planning, and safe steroid tapering.
  • Identify cortisol-excess findings and the complications that need surveillance.
  • Monitor for adrenal insufficiency after treatment of Cushing syndrome.

Understand the source of hormone deficiency

In primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), the adrenal cortex fails, so both cortisol and often aldosterone are deficient. Fatigue, weakness, weight loss, poor appetite, abdominal symptoms, dizziness or orthostatic hypotension, salt craving, and hyperpigmentation can occur. Hyponatremia, volume depletion, and hyperkalemia may be present, but no single finding confirms the diagnosis. Central adrenal insufficiency results from inadequate pituitary ACTH or hypothalamic stimulation; aldosterone is often relatively preserved, so hyperkalemia and marked salt wasting are less typical. Chronic exogenous glucocorticoids can suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis; abrupt withdrawal after sustained exposure may precipitate adrenal insufficiency. Ask about pills, inhaled or injected steroids, recent dose changes, surgery, and pituitary or adrenal disease. Confirm the diagnosis with ordered cortisol and ACTH-based testing; during a suspected crisis, do not delay emergency treatment while waiting for confirmatory results.

Adrenal crisis: recognize shock risk now

A client with known or possible adrenal insufficiency who becomes severely weak, vomiting, confused, hypotensive, or poorly perfused may be in adrenal crisis. Infection, trauma, surgery, inability to keep oral steroids down, or abrupt steroid interruption are common triggers. Hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, and sometimes hyperkalemia can add danger. Activate the emergency response and assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, glucose, ECG, urine output, and fluid status. Obtain ordered blood samples if immediately feasible, but samples must not postpone parenteral glucocorticoid treatment. Support prompt prescribed hydrocortisone, isotonic fluid resuscitation, glucose correction when needed, and treatment of the trigger. Monitor closely for dysrhythmias, persistent hypotension, electrolyte shifts, and fluid intolerance, especially with heart or kidney disease. A patient may need critical-care monitoring; the nurse should not assume routine oral steroid dosing will rescue shock.

Priority distinction
In stable outpatient assessment, tests help establish why cortisol is low. In suspected adrenal crisis, life-saving treatment takes precedence over a perfect diagnostic sample. Follow the local emergency pathway and authorized orders.

Long-term replacement and sick-day safety

Prescribed glucocorticoid replacement, often hydrocortisone in divided daily doses, replaces deficient cortisol. Primary adrenal insufficiency with aldosterone deficiency usually also needs fludrocortisone; most central insufficiency does not. Assess blood pressure including orthostatic symptoms, weight, edema, sodium, potassium, glucose, and medication access as directed. Review whether symptoms suggest under-replacement or excess replacement rather than changing the regimen independently. Teach the client never to stop replacement abruptly, to follow an individualized written illness or surgery stress-dose plan, and to seek urgent care for severe illness, injury, persistent vomiting or diarrhea, fainting, or inability to take oral medication. Confirm access to prescribed emergency injectable glucocorticoid and training for the client or caregiver, plus medical-alert identification and a steroid emergency card. Use teach-back: ask what the client would do if vomiting prevents the morning dose.

Recognize cortisol excess without assuming its cause

Cushing syndrome is prolonged excessive cortisol exposure. The commonest cause overall is prescribed glucocorticoid exposure; endogenous causes include pituitary ACTH excess (Cushing disease), ectopic ACTH, or an adrenal source. Central weight gain, rounded face, dorsocervical fat accumulation, thin limbs and proximal muscle weakness, easy bruising, wide purple striae, delayed wound healing, mood or sleep changes, and menstrual changes may occur. Assess hypertension, hyperglycemia, hypokalemia when present, infection, skin breakdown, osteoporosis or fracture, venous thromboembolism, and cardiovascular or psychiatric complications. These findings are not specific; diagnosis requires an appropriate clinical workup. Ask about all steroid routes, including injections and topical preparations, before labeling an endogenous syndrome. Nurses do not interpret a single random cortisol as definitive or encourage a client to stop a prescribed steroid on their own.

Treatment requires complication surveillance

The team treats the cause of endogenous cortisol excess, often with surgery when feasible, and may use cortisol-lowering medicines or radiation in selected cases. Nursing priorities before and after treatment include glucose and blood-pressure monitoring, infection assessment, skin protection, fall and fracture prevention, mental-health assessment, and evaluation for thrombosis symptoms. Sudden severe headache, focal deficit, chest pain, dyspnea, or unilateral leg swelling warrants urgent evaluation rather than attribution to a chronic endocrine problem. After successful tumor treatment or adrenal surgery, cortisol may become temporarily or permanently low; verify ordered replacement, stress-dose instructions, and monitoring. Bilateral adrenal removal requires lifelong adrenal-hormone replacement. When chronic prescribed glucocorticoids are the cause, dose reduction must be supervised and usually gradual enough to protect against withdrawal or adrenal insufficiency while still treating the original illness.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Trend blood pressure, perfusion, mentation, hydration, glucose, sodium, potassium, infection signs, weight and steroid history.
  2. Analyze cues: Consider primary, central or medication-induced cortisol deficiency versus cortisol excess, and look for a crisis trigger.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Shock, hypoglycemia, dangerous potassium changes, and inability to take replacement outrank routine diagnostic teaching.
  4. Generate solutions: Prepare monitored emergency support, confirm prescribed parenteral steroid and fluids, address the trigger, and plan safe ongoing replacement.
  5. Take action: Escalate suspected crisis immediately, obtain samples only if they do not delay treatment, administer ordered therapy, and reassess frequently.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Confirm improving perfusion, mentation, glucose and electrolytes; assess complications, replacement tolerance, and the client's ability to use the sick-day and emergency plan.

Clinical example

A client with Addison disease has influenza, repeated vomiting, dizziness, and blood pressure 78/46 mmHg. They cannot keep hydrocortisone tablets down. The RN recognizes possible adrenal crisis, calls for immediate emergency evaluation, checks glucose and cardiac status, supports ordered parenteral hydrocortisone and isotonic fluids without waiting for a cortisol result, and monitors perfusion and electrolytes. Before discharge, the team verifies an individualized sick-day plan, emergency injection access, and medical-alert identification.

Adrenal-crisis recognition, steroid dosing, fluid resuscitation, diagnostic testing, and treatment of cortisol excess require current patient data, authorized orders, local emergency protocols, and qualified supervision.
